lead: A wedge is a small triangular block driven under a load. It changes a modest horizontal push into a large normal force because its sloping face is a shallow inclined plane. Both the sloping face and the flat base are rough, so friction appears twice. Wedges lift machine beds, split wood, lock door stops and hold railway fishplates. The method is: separate the wedge and the load, draw both free bodies, and use the friction angle to find the push P needed to raise or lower the load, including self-locking.
prereq: You need: 3.4 friction laws and angle of friction and 3.5 inclined-plane equilibrium.

sections.h3: Two rough faces make the wedge

blocks.text: A wedge has a small angle α between its sloping face and its horizontal base. A load W rests on the sloping face. A horizontal push P drives the wedge forward, and the load rises along the slope. The load moves a short vertical distance while the wedge moves a longer horizontal distance. That is the force multiplication.

Both faces are rough. On the sloping face, the wedge pushes the load with normal N₁ and friction μN₁. On the floor, the floor pushes the wedge with normal N₂ and friction μN₂. Ignoring either friction gives a wrong P. A wedge is not a one-face inclined plane.

items: A wedge under a machine leg levels the machine.
A pair of wedges adjusts a machine-tool slide.
A door wedge holds a door open.
A splitting wedge turns a hammer blow into large pressure inside wood.

blocks.text: Draw the block and the wedge as separate free bodies. The block is held by a smooth vertical guide, so it moves only vertically. The guide gives a horizontal reaction H but no friction.

On the block: W acts down. The wedge gives normal N₁ perpendicular to the sloping face and friction f₁ = μN₁ down the slope, opposing the block's upward slip. Vertical equilibrium gives N₁ cos α − f₁ sin α = W.
On the wedge: the block's normal and friction reverse. The floor gives normal N₂ up and friction f₂ = μN₂ to the left, opposite the wedge's motion. At impending slip, use f₁ = μN₁ and f₂ = μN₂.
P = N₁ sin α + f₁ cos α + f₂
blocks.where: P is the horizontal push on the wedge; N₁ is the normal on the sloping face; f₁ = μN₁ is the friction on that face; f₂ = μN₂ is the floor friction; α is the wedge angle. The block presses back on the slope, so the normal component N₁ sin α and both friction components all resist the push.

blocks.text: Vertical equilibrium of the wedge gives N₂ = N₁ cos α − f₁ sin α. The block equation makes N₂ equal W in this arrangement. The friction angle φ = tan⁻¹ μ combines N and f on a face into one resultant R. R makes angle φ with the normal. On the wedge, P, R₁ from the block and R₂ from the floor form a force triangle.

Self-locking means the wedge stays in place after P is removed. Friction on both faces then holds the load. A small wedge angle and large friction help. To test it, set P = 0 and reverse both friction senses at the same time: the load now squeezes the wedge back out, so the block tends to slide down the slope, friction on the block acts up the slope, and both friction forces on the wedge reverse. Recompute N₁ and N₂, then find the floor friction needed. If that is within μN₂, the wedge is self-locking; if not, the wedge squeezes out.

Directions change with motion. For raising, friction on the block is down the slope. For lowering, friction on the block is up the slope and friction on the wedge reverses. Recompute both normals; do not reuse the raising signs.
A quick check on the numbers: N₁ is not W. While raising, N₁ = W / (cos α − μ sin α), so it is larger than W. The floor normal N₂ comes from wedge vertical equilibrium, not from a guess.

figure.caption: The block is guided vertically. Friction acts on the sloping face and on the floor, so the wedge free body has two friction forces and the push P must overcome both.

spec.title: Wedge free bodies
spec.aria: A wedge of angle 15 degrees under a 500 N block, with friction on both faces and a free-body diagram leading to the push P.

examples.question: A 15° wedge is driven under a 500 N block. The block is held by a smooth vertical guide. The coefficient of friction is 0.25 on the sloping face and 0.25 on the floor. Find the horizontal force P needed to raise the block.
steps: Given: wedge angle α = 15°, block weight W = 500 N, μ = 0.25 on both faces. The weight of the wedge is neglected and the guide is smooth, so the floor normal N₂ carries only the load transmitted from the block. The friction angle is φ = tan⁻¹(0.25) = 14.04°, but the equations do not need it.
For impending upward motion, friction on the block acts down the slope. Block vertical equilibrium: N₁ cos 15° − μN₁ sin 15° = W.
Wedge vertical equilibrium: N₂ + f₁ sin 15° = N₁ cos 15°. So N₂ = 554.80 × 0.9659 − 138.70 × 0.2588 = 500.0 N.
Wedge horizontal equilibrium: P = N₁ sin 15° + f₁ cos 15° + f₂ = 554.80 × 0.2588 + 138.70 × 0.9659 + 125.0. The block's normal pushes the wedge back out, so its horizontal component adds to the push.
examples.answer: The horizontal push needed to raise the block is P = 402.56 N ≈ 402.6 N in the direction of the push.
examples.check:
import math
W = 500.0
alpha = math.radians(15)
mu = 0.25
N1 = W / (math.cos(alpha) - mu * math.sin(alpha))
f1 = mu * N1
N2 = N1 * math.cos(alpha) - f1 * math.sin(alpha)
f2 = mu * N2
P = f1 * math.cos(alpha) + f2 + N1 * math.sin(alpha)
print(f"{N1:.2f}")
print(f"{f1:.2f}")
print(f"{N2:.2f}")
print(f"{f2:.2f}")
print(f"{P:.2f}")

traps: Showing friction on only the sloping face. The floor under the wedge is also rough; f₂ = μN₂ adds to the push P.
Taking N₁ equal to W. The sloping normal is N₁ = W / (cos α − μ sin α) while raising, so it is larger than W.
Using the raising friction directions for lowering. Reverse friction on both faces when the block is being lowered.
Mixing the wedge angle with the friction angle. α sets the slope; φ = tan⁻¹ μ sets the tilt of the resultant reaction.
Forgetting the smooth guide reaction H. It does not enter P here, but it keeps the block from moving sideways.

quiz.q: What is a wedge, and on which two faces does friction act in a wedge problem?
quiz.a: A wedge is a small-angle triangular block used to lift or hold a load. Friction acts on the sloping face between wedge and load, and on the base between wedge and floor.

quiz.q: Why can the normal N₁ on the sloping face be larger than the block weight W?
quiz.a: Because N₁ must balance W and also the component of friction along the slope. For raising, N₁ = W / (cos α − μ sin α), which is greater than W for usual values of α and μ.

quiz.q: In the worked example, compute f₁ and f₂.
quiz.a: N₁ = 554.80 N, so f₁ = μN₁ = 138.70 N. N₂ = 500.0 N, so f₂ = μN₂ = 125.0 N.

quiz.q: For the worked example, write the two equations that give P, with numbers inserted.
quiz.a: Block vertical: N₁ cos 15° − 0.25N₁ sin 15° = 500. Wedge horizontal: P = N₁ sin 15° + 0.25N₁ cos 15° + 0.25N₂, with N₁ = 554.80 N and N₂ = 500 N, giving P = 143.59 + 133.97 + 125.0 = 402.56 N.

quiz.q: After the block is raised, P is removed. What floor friction is needed to hold the wedge? Is the wedge self-locking?
quiz.a: With P removed the load squeezes the wedge back out, so the block tends to slide down the slope and friction on it acts up the slope; both friction forces on the wedge reverse. Block vertical: N₁(cos 15° + 0.25 sin 15°) = 500, so N₁ = 485.2 N and f₁ = 121.3 N. Wedge vertical: N₂ = N₁ cos 15° + f₁ sin 15° = 500 N. Floor friction needed: f₂ = N₁ sin 15° − f₁ cos 15° = 125.6 − 117.2 = 8.4 N, well within μN₂ = 125 N. The wedge is self-locking.

quiz.q: Why must you reverse friction arrows when the block is lowered rather than raised?
quiz.a: Friction opposes impending relative motion. In raising, the block tends to move up the slope, so friction on it acts down. In lowering it tends down, so friction on it acts up; the force on the wedge also reverses. Using raising arrows gives a wrong P.

quiz.q: A wedge has a large angle and polished faces. Is it likely to be self-locking? Explain.
quiz.a: No. A large angle gives a steep slope, and low friction gives little resistance. With P removed, the load can push the wedge out. Self-locking favours a small wedge angle and high friction.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wedge friction appears in clamps, taper pins, machine-tool levelling and railway fastenings. A tapered joint is designed to be self-locking so vibration does not loosen it, yet release with a deliberate pull. The same friction-angle idea leads to the screw jack, where an inclined plane is wrapped round a cylinder. Search 'self-locking taper', 'wedge friction force triangle' and 'friction angle wedge'.
